title: Why mentor training cannot be one-size-fits-all
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Haili Hughes argues that schools treat mentors as interchangeable, assuming good teachers make good mentors and that one generic training session suffices, and she includes the ECF and ITT mentor programmes in her critique for flattening mentoring into generic competencies. Drawing on a study of 367 preservice teachers, she highlights the gap between what novices expected and what they received, which was largest in professional guidance: feedback, dialogue, identity and career development. Mentors tend to be good at practical preparation but weaker at helping novices understand and reflect on decisions, which she links to a recent obsession with 'action steps' over the why. She argues mentors start from different places, that seniority is not mentoring skill (mid-career mentors were rated highest), that mentoring comprises distinct competences, and that weak mentoring is mainly about competence rather than context. She warns against an apprenticeship model that produces imitation rather than judgement. Schools should diagnose what kinds of mentors they need and differentiate training by mentor stage.
points: A study of 367 preservice teachers found the biggest gap between expectation and reality lay in professional guidance, not practical lesson preparation.
Hughes links this to a mentoring culture fixated on 'action steps' that rarely addresses the why behind teaching decisions.
Seniority is not mentoring skill: mentors with 11-20 years' experience were rated above those at the start or end of their careers, so selection should not rest on years served.
Copying the mentor may yield compliance and surface polish but not judgement; growth requires dialogue about alternatives and the reasoning behind choices.
Mentor development should be differentiated by stage, with structures for new mentors, coaching and dialogue refinement for mid-career mentors, and assumption-revisiting for veterans.
quotes: Like everything in education, we have tried to flatten and steam-roller mentor training into a generic set of competencies, which often do not take into account mentor experience or context. To be fair though, I don’t think we should throw out the baby with the bath water and what we have now for mentors in terms of training is so much better than the logistical paperwork training we used to have in the UK.

This comes as no surprise to me. We have become so obsessed with the what and how of teaching in the last few years that most mentoring conversations I hear focus on ‘action steps’ and not really the why.
That distinction matters because mentoring is not just supervision. It is not just checking plans, signing forms, or giving tips. If that is all you do, you may help someone survive the placement.

Some are experienced teachers but inexperienced mentors. They may know how to teach well but struggle to explain their own decisions. They may do things intuitively and find it hard to make that thinking visible to a novice.
A mentor may be strong in one area and weak in another. One mentor may help a novice plan well but give poor feedback. Another may be encouraging but imprecise.
That is a weak model of professional learning. It may produce compliance. It may even produce surface polish.
A flat model of mentor training ignores the obvious. People at different stages need different things.
